{{Short description|Set of computational problems stated by Richard Karp (1973)}}

In [[computational complexity theory]], '''Karp's 21 NP-complete problems''' are a set of [[computational problem]]s which are [[NP-complete]]. In his 1972 paper, "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems",{{sfn |Karp|1972}} [[Richard Karp]] used [[Stephen Cook]]'s 1971 theorem that the [[Boolean satisfiability problem]] is NP-complete{{sfn |Cook|1971}} (also called the [[Cook–Levin theorem]]) to show that there is a [[polynomial time]] [[many-one reduction]] from the Boolean satisfiability problem to each of 21 [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] and [[graph theory|graph theoretical]] computational problems, thereby showing that they are all NP-complete. This was one of the first demonstrations that many natural computational problems occurring throughout [[computer science]] are [[computationally intractable]], and it drove interest in the study of NP-completeness and the [[P versus NP problem]].

== The problems ==
Karp's 21 problems are shown below, many with their original names. The nesting indicates the direction of the reductions used. For example, '''[[Knapsack problem|Knapsack]]''' was shown to be NP-complete by reducing '''[[Exact cover]]''' to '''Knapsack'''.

* '''[[Boolean satisfiability problem|Satisfiability]]''': the Boolean satisfiability problem for formulas in [[conjunctive normal form]] (often referred to as SAT)
** '''[[Integer linear programming|0–1 integer programming]]''' (A variation in which only the restrictions must be satisfied, with no optimization)
** '''[[Clique problem|Clique]]''' (see also [[independent set problem]])
*** '''[[Set packing]]'''
*** '''[[Vertex cover problem|Vertex cover]]'''
**** '''[[Set cover problem|Set covering]]'''
**** '''[[Feedback vertex set|Feedback node set]]'''
**** '''[[Feedback arc set]]'''
**** '''[[Hamiltonian path problem|Directed Hamilton circuit]]''' (Karp's name, now usually called '''Directed Hamiltonian cycle''')
***** '''[[Hamiltonian path problem|Undirected Hamilton circuit]]''' (Karp's name, now usually called '''Undirected Hamiltonian cycle''')
** '''[[Boolean satisfiability problem#3-satisfiability|Satisfiability with at most 3 literals per clause]]''' (equivalent to 3-SAT)
*** '''[[Graph coloring|Chromatic number]]''' (also called the [[Graph coloring|Graph Coloring Problem]])
**** '''[[Clique cover]]'''
**** '''[[Exact cover]]'''
***** '''[[Hitting set]]'''
***** '''[[Steiner tree problem|Steiner tree]]'''
***** '''[[3-dimensional matching]]'''
***** '''[[Knapsack problem|Knapsack]]''' (Karp's definition of Knapsack is closer to [[Subset sum]])
****** '''[[Job shop scheduling|Job sequencing]]'''
****** '''[[Partition problem|Partition]]'''
******* '''[[Maximum cut|Max cut]]'''

== Approximations ==
As time went on it was discovered that many of the problems can be solved efficiently if restricted to special cases, or can be solved within any fixed percentage of the optimal result. However, [[David Zuckerman (mathematician)|David Zuckerman]] showed in 1996 that every one of these 21 problems has a constrained optimization version that is impossible to approximate within any constant factor unless P = NP, by showing that Karp's approach to reduction generalizes to a specific type of approximability reduction.{{sfn |Zuckerman|1996}} However, these may be different from the standard optimization versions of the problems, which may have approximation algorithms (as in the case of maximum cut).
